# Abstract

Successful communication depends not just on what we say but also on how we repair it when understanding breaks down. People routinely respond to misunderstanding by gesturing more or speaking louder. Yet whether these responses actually reflect measurable bodily effort, and whether it helps communication, has not, to our knowledge, been directly tested. Extending the hypo- and hyper-articulation accounts to whole-body multimodal communication we ask: does regaining understanding require increased physical effort, and does that effort improve communicative outcomes? In a pre-registered biomechanical study, 61 pairs of participants conveyed concepts without language, using gestures, voice, or both, and repaired failed attempts. We measured effort directly as arm torque, vocal amplitude, and postural adjustments. Using Bayesian hierarchical models, we show that repair increases physical effort across all three channels, but that performers communicate more over time rather than more forcefully at any particular moment in time. Upper-limb effort scales with the degree of misunderstanding but this does not predict whether communication succeeds. We suggest that effort functions as an index of continued commitment rather than a mechanism for repairing misunderstanding.
